prompt: Which statement best defines a free good?

options.label: A
options.text: No scarcity and no opportunity cost

options.label: B
options.text: It is purchased at a price below its cost of production.

options.label: C
options.text: It is supplied by the government at a zero price.

options.label: D
options.text: It is non-excludable but must be scarce.

explanation: A free good is abundant relative to the relevant wants, so obtaining another unit does not sacrifice an alternative use of scarce resources.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which pair of characteristics is associated with a private good?

options.label: A
options.text: Non-excludable and rival in consumption

options.label: B
options.text: Excludable and non-rival in consumption

options.label: C
options.text: Non-excludable and non-rival in consumption

options.label: D
options.text: Excludable and rival in consumption

explanation: A seller can exclude someone who does not obtain the good, and consuming a unit leaves fewer units for others. These are excludability and rivalry.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What are the two defining characteristics of a public good?

options.label: A
options.text: Scarcity and rivalry

options.label: B
options.text: Non-excludability and non-rivalry

options.label: C
options.text: Excludability and scarcity

options.label: D
options.text: Zero price and government ownership

explanation: Public goods combine access that cannot feasibly exclude non-payers with benefits that do not diminish when another person uses them.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why may a merit good be under-consumed in a market?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers always face a zero price.

options.label: B
options.text: Consumption by one person always reduces consumption by another.

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers underestimate their personal benefits.

options.label: D
options.text: Producers are unable to exclude non-payers.

explanation: Underestimated personal benefits make consumers choose less than they would with accurate information. This is the merit-good information problem.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why may a demerit good be over-consumed in a market?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers underestimate their personal harms.

options.label: B
options.text: Producers cannot charge a price for it.

options.label: C
options.text: It is always non-rival in consumption.

options.label: D
options.text: It has no opportunity cost.

explanation: If buyers overlook personal harm, they may choose more than they would after learning the risks. This creates demerit-good over-consumption.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.4 nature and definition of demerit goods: over-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which is most likely to be a free good in an economy where it is naturally abundant?

options.label: A
options.text: Sunlight

options.label: B
options.text: Bottled drinking water

options.label: C
options.text: A school textbook

options.label: D
options.text: A cinema ticket

explanation: Naturally abundant sunlight is the only listed item whose additional use need not sacrifice scarce resources. Water bottles, textbooks and cinema seats require resources.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A vaccination is provided to patients without charge, but doctors, buildings and medical supplies are required to provide it. What does this show?

options.label: A
options.text: The vaccination cannot be a merit good.

options.label: B
options.text: The vaccination must be a public good.

options.label: C
options.text: The vaccination has zero opportunity cost.

options.label: D
options.text: A zero price does not make it a free good.

explanation: Doctors, buildings and supplies have alternative uses. Providing vaccination without a patient charge changes who pays, not its opportunity cost.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which service is most likely to satisfy both conditions for a public good?

options.label: A
options.text: A meal in a restaurant

options.label: B
options.text: National defence

options.label: C
options.text: A pay-per-view sports broadcast

options.label: D
options.text: A seat on a train

explanation: One resident's protection does not reduce another's, and residents cannot feasibly be excluded individually. A meal, paid broadcast or train seat fails at least one condition.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A sandwich bought from a shop is best described as a private good because it is

options.label: A
options.text: Non-excludable and non-rival in consumption.

options.label: B
options.text: Free at the point of use.

options.label: C
options.text: Under-consumed because of imperfect information.

options.label: D
options.text: Excludable and rival in consumption.

explanation: The shop can deny the sandwich to a non-buyer, and eating it prevents another person from eating the same sandwich.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What does non-rival consumption mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The good has no opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: An extra user's consumption does not reduce the benefit to others.

options.label: C
options.text: The government is the only possible provider.

options.label: D
options.text: A provider can prevent non-payers from consuming the good by requiring each user to buy access.

explanation: Non-rivalry concerns the effect on other users: an additional user's consumption does not reduce the benefit already available to them.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What does non-excludability mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The good must be supplied at a zero price.

options.label: B
options.text: Consumption by one person reduces the amount available to others.

options.label: C
options.text: Non-payers cannot feasibly be prevented from benefiting.

options.label: D
options.text: The good uses no scarce resources.

explanation: Non-excludability means access cannot feasibly be withheld from someone who does not pay. It does not imply costless production.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why is a private good also described as an economic good?

options.label: A
options.text: It must be supplied by a profit-maximising firm.

options.label: B
options.text: It is always a necessity.

options.label: C
options.text: It is scarce and has an opportunity cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Its price is always greater than zero.

explanation: Private goods are scarce, so resources devoted to supplying them have alternative uses. Government provision or a zero user price would not remove this cost.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Consumers are unaware of many of the long-term benefits of preventive dental checks. Which classification is most consistent with this information?

options.label: A
options.text: A merit good

options.label: B
options.text: A public good

options.label: C
options.text: A demerit good

options.label: D
options.text: A free good

explanation: Unawareness of preventive dental benefits can depress demand below the fully informed quantity. That supports classification as a merit good.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Consumers do not realise the long-term health damage caused by a particular product and buy more of it than they would if fully informed. What type of good is described?

options.label: A
options.text: A merit good

options.label: B
options.text: A free good

options.label: C
options.text: A public good

options.label: D
options.text: A demerit good

explanation: Consumers overlook health damage and buy more than their fully informed choice. The excessive quantity arises from a demerit-good information failure.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.4 nature and definition of demerit goods: over-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A beach charges every visitor an entrance fee and has limited space. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: It must be a merit good.

options.label: B
options.text: It must be a free good.

options.label: C
options.text: It is not a pure public good.

options.label: D
options.text: It is non-excludable because being located outdoors prevents the operator from restricting entry to paying visitors.

explanation: The entrance fee permits exclusion, and limited beach space may create rivalry. The beach therefore cannot meet both pure-public-good conditions.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which feature of national defence makes it non-rival?

options.label: A
options.text: Only taxpayers receive protection.

options.label: B
options.text: One resident's protection does not reduce another's.

options.label: C
options.text: National defence uses no scarce resources.

options.label: D
options.text: Residents can be charged different prices for protection.

explanation: Protection extends to an additional resident without taking protection away from existing residents. That identifies non-rivalry, rather than a rule about who pays.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A digital streaming service can block access to anyone who does not pay. Even if an extra viewer does not reduce the quality available to others, why is it not a pure public good?

options.label: A
options.text: It is non-rival.

options.label: B
options.text: It is excludable.

options.label: C
options.text: It is produced by a private firm.

options.label: D
options.text: It has a monetary price.

explanation: Blocking non-paying viewers establishes excludability. Even with non-rival viewing, the streaming service fails one necessary public-good condition.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement about a free good is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It must be provided by the state.

options.label: B
options.text: It has zero opportunity cost when genuinely abundant.

options.label: C
options.text: It must be a merit good.

options.label: D
options.text: It must be non-excludable and non-rival.

explanation: Genuine abundance makes the next unit available without sacrificing another valued resource use. A zero price or state provider alone does not establish this.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Air in an open rural area is initially abundant. Later, specialised equipment and scarce labour are needed to supply clean air inside a sealed facility. What has changed?

options.label: A
options.text: Supplied clean air becomes economic because production uses scarce resources.

options.label: B
options.text: Clean air supplied inside the facility remains a free good because air elsewhere is abundant, despite the resources needed for purification.

options.label: C
options.text: Supplied clean air becomes demerit because production requires scarce resources.

options.label: D
options.text: Supplied clean air becomes public because every worker needs it.

explanation: Supplying clean air to the facility now requires equipment and labour with alternative uses. The supplied service is economic despite abundant air outside.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A service is owned and operated by a government. What can be concluded from this information alone?

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot be a private good.

options.label: B
options.text: Ownership alone does not determine whether it is a public good.

options.label: C
options.text: It must be a free good.

options.label: D
options.text: It must be a public good because government ownership guarantees that users cannot be excluded and consumption is non-rival.

explanation: Ownership tells us who operates the service. Whether non-payers can be excluded and whether use is rival must be examined separately.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A bus journey requires a ticket and one passenger can occupy a seat that another passenger could have used. How is the journey best classified?

options.label: A
options.text: A free good

options.label: B
options.text: A demerit good

options.label: C
options.text: A public good

options.label: D
options.text: A private good

explanation: Ticket checks can exclude passengers, and an occupied seat is unavailable to another traveller. These excludable, rival consumption characteristics make the journey a private good.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which characteristic would prevent a service from being a pure public good?

options.label: A
options.text: Non-payers can be excluded.

options.label: B
options.text: It uses scarce resources.

options.label: C
options.text: An additional user does not reduce its benefit.

options.label: D
options.text: It is valued by consumers.

explanation: Excluding non-payers contradicts non-excludability, a necessary public-good condition. Using resources or being valued does not contradict the definition.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A school place can be restricted to enrolled students and there is a limit to the number of places. It may nevertheless be a merit good. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A merit good must have zero opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Every private good is a demerit good.

options.label: C
options.text: It can be both a private good and a merit good.

options.label: D
options.text: Every merit good necessarily meets the non-excludability and non-rivalry conditions required for classification as a public good.

explanation: Enrolment permits exclusion and limited places create rivalry. Underestimating schooling's benefits can also make the same service a merit good.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a merit good from a demerit good?

options.label: A
options.text: Imperfect information: merit under-consumed; demerit over-consumed.

options.label: B
options.text: Excludability: merit non-excludable; demerit excludable.

options.label: C
options.text: Rivalry: merit non-rival; demerit rival.

options.label: D
options.text: Opportunity cost: merit free; demerit scarce.

explanation: The distinction is the direction of the information-related consumption error: too little from understated benefits versus too much from understated harm.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | 1.6.4 nature and definition of demerit goods: over-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A product is distributed without charge by a charity, but it is scarce and one person consuming it leaves less for others. What is the best conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: A zero price does not make it a free good.

options.label: B
options.text: It is non-rival because it is donated.

options.label: C
options.text: It must be a public good because charitable provision makes the product non-rival even when the available stock is limited.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a free good because nobody pays.

explanation: Donating the scarce product does not make its production costless. Its rival use and forgone alternative applications remain despite the zero price.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO2 Analysis

prompt:
Which row correctly matches the good with its defining characteristic?
| Good | Defining idea |
| Free good | ? |
| Public good | ? |

options.label: A
options.text: Free goods: services provided by government authorities; public goods: services with no opportunity cost regardless of scarcity.

options.label: B
options.text: Free: under-consumed; public: over-consumed from imperfect information.

options.label: C
options.text: Free: no opportunity cost; public: non-excludable and non-rival.

options.label: D
options.text: Free: non-excludable and scarce; public: excludable and rival.

explanation: Free goods are classified by zero opportunity cost. Public goods are classified by non-excludability and non-rivalry, regardless of their production costs.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why is it usually difficult to charge each user directly for a pure public good?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers always underestimate its benefits.

options.label: B
options.text: Non-payers cannot feasibly be excluded.

options.label: C
options.text: Consumption is always rival.

options.label: D
options.text: The good has no production cost.

explanation: A supplier cannot feasibly withhold a pure public good's benefit from non-payers. This undermines collecting a separate voluntary payment from every beneficiary.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Atmospheric oxygen is abundant, while oxygen supplied in a hospital cylinder uses equipment and scarce resources. Which classification is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Atmospheric oxygen: free; cylinder oxygen: economic

options.label: B
options.text: Both are public goods because breathing is essential.

options.label: C
options.text: Cylinder oxygen is a demerit good because it has a price.

options.label: D
options.text: Both are free goods because both contain oxygen.

explanation: Abundant atmospheric oxygen can be used without a resource sacrifice. Delivering cylinder oxygen requires scarce equipment and resources, making that supplied product economic.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A health screening service is consumed less than it would be if people understood its full personal benefits. This is an example of

options.label: A
options.text: A demerit good whose consumers obtain too much because they do not fully understand the personal harm associated with it.

options.label: B
options.text: A merit good being under-consumed because of imperfect information.

options.label: C
options.text: A free good becoming scarce.

options.label: D
options.text: A public good being under-provided because it is non-rival.

explanation: People obtain less screening because they underestimate personal benefits. The gap between actual and informed consumption is the merit-good mechanism.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Consumers purchase many high-caffeine drinks because they are unaware of some health risks. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The drinks are a public good because many people consume them.

options.label: B
options.text: It may be a demerit good because of information failure.

options.label: C
options.text: The drinks are a free good if the price is low.

options.label: D
options.text: The drinks are a merit good because consumers value them.

explanation: Missing knowledge of health risks may inflate demand for high-caffeine drinks. This supports a demerit-good explanation rather than one based simply on high sales.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.4 nature and definition of demerit goods: over-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A museum has free admission, but staff, security and buildings are scarce resources. Which conclusion is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The museum service has no opportunity cost to society.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum service must be a public good because it is cultural.

options.label: C
options.text: Zero admission does not make it a free good.

options.label: D
options.text: The museum service must be a free good because its price is zero.

explanation: Museum staff, security and buildings could be used elsewhere. Free admission removes a visitor charge but leaves the service's opportunity cost intact.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A road bridge can be crossed only after a toll is paid. What does the toll most clearly demonstrate?

options.label: A
options.text: The service is a free good.

options.label: B
options.text: The service is non-rival.

options.label: C
options.text: The service is excludable.

options.label: D
options.text: The service must be a merit good.

explanation: A toll can be enforced by denying a crossing to non-payers. It demonstrates excludability without establishing whether bridge use is rival.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A road cannot exclude users, but at peak time one extra vehicle increases congestion for others. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The road must be a free good because no toll is charged.

options.label: B
options.text: The road is a merit good because it is useful.

options.label: C
options.text: The road remains non-rival at peak times because unrestricted entry means extra vehicles cannot reduce the benefits other drivers receive.

options.label: D
options.text: It is not a pure public good because consumption becomes rival.

explanation: Another vehicle worsens congestion for existing drivers. Rivalry at peak times prevents the road from being a pure public good, despite unrestricted entry.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: An emergency warning signal can be received by every household in a region. No household can be excluded and one more household receiving it does not reduce anyone else’s benefit. How should the signal be classified?

options.label: A
options.text: A demerit good

options.label: B
options.text: A public good

options.label: C
options.text: A private good

options.label: D
options.text: A free good

explanation: All households can receive the warning, and additional reception leaves others' benefits unchanged. Both defining public-good conditions are satisfied.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A research database can be used by many subscribers at the same time without reducing its usefulness, but access is password-protected. Which characteristic stops it being a pure public good?

options.label: A
options.text: Scarcity

options.label: B
options.text: Excludability

options.label: C
options.text: Imperfect information

options.label: D
options.text: Non-rivalry

explanation: Password protection lets the provider exclude non-subscribers. The database's non-rival use is insufficient to make it a pure public good.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A radio signal was previously impossible to restrict to paying users. New technology now allows receivers to decode it only after payment. Other users are still unaffected by one extra listener. What is the main classification change?

options.label: A
options.text: It becomes a free good because listeners do not compete.

options.label: B
options.text: It becomes rival in consumption.

options.label: C
options.text: It becomes a merit good because technology improved.

options.label: D
options.text: It becomes excludable, so it is no longer a pure public good.

explanation: Decoding now depends on payment, so non-payers can be excluded. Consumption remains non-rival, but the service no longer satisfies the full public-good definition.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Groundwater is not priced in a village, but the available supply is limited during a drought. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The water is a demerit good because it is limited.

options.label: B
options.text: It is an economic good because the drought makes it scarce.

options.label: C
options.text: The water is a free good because villagers do not pay for it.

options.label: D
options.text: The water is a public good because all villagers need it.

explanation: Drought creates competing demands for limited groundwater. Its opportunity cost is positive even though villagers face no monetary charge.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which situation provides the strongest example of a free good?

options.label: A
options.text: Sunlight that is abundant enough to have zero opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Emergency hospital treatment provided without charging patients but requiring scarce medical staff, equipment and buildings.

options.label: C
options.text: A charity gives away a limited stock of blankets.

options.label: D
options.text: A council provides free school meals financed by taxation.

explanation: Abundant sunlight is explicitly available without opportunity cost. Treatment, blankets and meals instead require scarce staff, supplies or food.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A town previously obtained clean river water without using scarce resources. Pollution later means water must be treated with labour and machinery before use. What is the best conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: Treated water becomes a public good because everyone benefits from water.

options.label: B
options.text: It is now an economic good because treatment uses scarce resources.

options.label: C
options.text: Treated water becomes a demerit good because pollution exists.

options.label: D
options.text: Treated water remains a free good because the river itself is natural.

explanation: Labour and machinery used for treatment have alternative applications. The treated water is an economic product even if untreated river water was previously abundant.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: After receiving reliable information about the benefits of a preventive health check, more consumers choose to obtain it. What does this evidence suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: The health check must be a public good.

options.label: B
options.text: Earlier consumption was consistent with under-consumption of a merit good.

options.label: C
options.text: Earlier consumption must have been above the informed level, consistent with a demerit good.

options.label: D
options.text: The health check must have zero opportunity cost.

explanation: More purchases after learning the benefits are consistent with previously underestimated benefits. That supports earlier merit-good under-consumption, rather than public-good classification.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: After accurate warning labels are introduced, consumers reduce their consumption of a product. What is the strongest inference if the change occurs because consumers now understand previously unknown personal health risks?

options.label: A
options.text: The product must have been under-consumed as a merit good because any reduction in demand reveals underestimated personal benefits.

options.label: B
options.text: The product is a public good because information is shared.

options.label: C
options.text: The product is a free good because information changed demand.

options.label: D
options.text: Earlier consumption was consistent with over-consumption of a demerit good.

explanation: Learning previously unknown health risks reduces desired consumption. Earlier demand may therefore have exceeded the fully informed quantity, consistent with a demerit good.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.4 nature and definition of demerit goods: over-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement about classifications is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers of every private good have perfect information.

options.label: B
options.text: A private good can also be a merit good.

options.label: C
options.text: A good cannot belong to more than one classification.

options.label: D
options.text: Every merit good must be non-excludable.

explanation: Private status concerns exclusion and rivalry; merit status concerns underestimated benefits. A good can satisfy both descriptions at once.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is the key difference between a free good and a public good?

options.label: A
options.text: A free good is supplied by firms, whereas a public good is supplied only by governments.

options.label: B
options.text: A free good is under-consumed, whereas a public good is over-consumed.

options.label: C
options.text: A free good is always rival, whereas a public good is always excludable.

options.label: D
options.text: Free goods have zero opportunity cost; public goods may use scarce resources.

explanation: Free goods have no opportunity cost in the relevant setting. Public goods can require scarce resources even though non-payers cannot be excluded from non-rival benefits.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A government-owned swimming pool limits entry to ticket holders and has a fixed safe capacity. How should the swimming service be classified by its consumption characteristics?

options.label: A
options.text: As a public good because the government owns it

options.label: B
options.text: A private/economic service: excludable and rival

options.label: C

explanation: The decisive condition is zero opportunity cost in the relevant setting. Neither ownership, consumer information nor public-good characteristics defines a free good.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement must be true of a private good?

options.label: A
options.text: It is excludable and rival in consumption.

options.label: B
options.text: It is always a demerit good.

options.label: C
options.text: It must be produced exclusively by privately owned firms, because publicly owned providers cannot supply excludable goods.

options.label: D
options.text: It has no opportunity cost if given away.

explanation: Private-good consumption allows exclusion and is rival. Public providers can supply such goods, and giving them away does not remove resource scarcity.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement must be true of a pure public good?

options.label: A
options.text: It is produced by the public sector.

options.label: B
options.text: It is provided at zero social cost.

options.label: C
options.text: It is under-consumed because of imperfect information.

options.label: D
options.text: It is non-excludable and non-rival.

explanation: Both non-excludability and non-rivalry are required. Government ownership and zero social cost are not part of the pure-public-good definition.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Consumers buy too little of a service solely because they do not understand its personal benefits. Which classification is justified by that information?

options.label: A
options.text: Demerit good

options.label: B
options.text: Free good

options.label: C
options.text: Public good

options.label: D
options.text: Merit good

explanation: The stated cause of too little consumption is underestimated personal benefit. That is enough to identify the merit-good information mechanism.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Consumers reduce use of a product after receiving accurate information about a previously unknown personal health risk. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: A
options.text: Previous use demonstrates that the product had zero opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Previous use is consistent with under-consumption from underestimated personal benefits.

options.label: C
options.text: Previous use demonstrates that the product was non-excludable and non-rival.

options.label: D
options.text: Previous use is consistent with over-consumption from underestimated personal harm.

explanation: Correct risk information lowers use, supporting earlier demand above the fully informed level. This is the demerit-good mechanism rather than merit-good under-consumption.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.4 nature and definition of demerit goods: over-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A service cannot exclude users, but as more people consume it each existing user receives less benefit. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: It is not a pure public good because consumption is rival.

options.label: B
options.text: It must be a pure public good because non-excludability is sufficient even though extra users reduce the benefits existing users receive.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a free good because access is open.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a merit good because many people want it.

explanation: Additional users reduce existing users' benefits, so consumption is rival. Open access alone cannot establish a pure public good.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A charity distributes a limited number of meals at no charge. Each meal eaten by one person cannot be eaten by someone else. What is the strongest conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: The meals are free goods because their price is zero.

options.label: B
options.text: The meals are economic/private goods even though recipients pay no price.

options.label: C
options.text: The meals are non-rival because recipients do not compete through prices.

options.label: D
options.text: The meals are public goods because a charity supplies them.

explanation: Meals are limited and each eaten meal is unavailable to others. The charity allocates scarce private goods; a zero recipient price does not make them free goods.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which distinction is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Public goods can be scarce; free goods have no opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Public goods are necessarily desirable; free goods are necessarily harmful.

options.label: C
options.text: Public goods have no price; free goods have a positive price.

options.label: D
options.text: Public goods are rival; free goods are non-rival in consumption.

explanation: Supplying non-excludable, non-rival benefits can still use scarce resources. A free good is distinguished by zero opportunity cost, not desirability or ownership.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government advertises “free education”. School places require teachers and buildings, and places can be restricted to enrolled students. Consumers may nevertheless obtain too little education if they underestimate its benefits. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The education is a demerit good because places are scarce.

options.label: B
options.text: The education is a free good because students pay nothing.

options.label: C
options.text: The education is a public good because government provides it.

options.label: D
options.text: It is an economic service and may also be a merit good.

explanation: Teachers and buildings make schooling economic despite zero tuition charges. Underestimated educational benefits can also support a merit-good explanation for low uptake.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.1 nature and definition of free goods and private goods (economic goods) | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Consumers are fully informed about all personal benefits of a service but buy little of it because its market price is high. Can the low consumption alone justify classifying it as a merit good?

options.label: A
options.text: No; merit-good under-consumption must arise from imperfect information.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because every service with low consumption is a merit good.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because high prices make a good public.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because merit goods must have zero prices.

explanation: High prices can constrain fully informed consumers without creating an information error. Low consumption alone therefore does not establish the specified merit-good mechanism.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Consumers are fully informed about all personal risks of a product but choose to consume a large quantity. Can high consumption alone establish that the product is a demerit good?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes; any product consumed in large quantities must be a demerit good even if consumers understand all its personal risks.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because demerit goods must be free goods.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because informed choice makes the good public.

options.label: D
options.text: No; demerit-good over-consumption must arise from imperfect information.

explanation: Fully informed high consumption does not show demand distorted by underestimated personal risks. More evidence is needed to establish the demerit-good information mechanism.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.4 nature and definition of demerit goods: over-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A private company supplies a service that is impossible to exclude people from using and for which one extra user does not reduce anyone else’s benefit. What is the best classification?

options.label: A
options.text: Public good

options.label: B
options.text: Private good

options.label: C
options.text: Free good

options.label: D
options.text: Demerit good

explanation: The service meets both public-good conditions regardless of the supplying company's ownership. Private provision does not make its benefits excludable or rival.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which criterion is most relevant when distinguishing a merit good from a demerit good?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether the good is rival or non-rival.

options.label: B
options.text: Whether the monetary price is high or low.

options.label: C
options.text: Whether information failure causes under- or over-consumption.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether the organisation supplying the product belongs to the public sector or is owned by private investors.

explanation: Merit and demerit classifications concern the direction of information-related consumption errors. Price levels, ownership and rivalry are separate characteristics.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.3 nature and definition of merit goods: under-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | 1.6.4 nature and definition of demerit goods: over-consumption as a result of imperfect information in the market | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A road is open to all vehicles, access cannot be restricted, and traffic is so light that an additional car does not slow any other driver. Which classification is most consistent with these facts?

options.label: A
options.text: Public good

options.label: B
options.text: Private good

options.label: C
options.text: Free good

options.label: D
options.text: Demerit good

explanation: Unrestricted access establishes non-excludability, and light traffic leaves additional use non-rival. The road has public-good characteristics in this stated setting.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An emergency broadcast can be received simultaneously by any number of users, but it is encrypted so that only paying subscribers can receive it. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a free good because broadcasting one more signal costs little.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a pure public good because it is non-rival.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a merit good because emergencies are important.

options.label: D
options.text: It is non-rival but excludable, so it is not a pure public good.

explanation: Encryption excludes non-subscribers. Despite non-rival reception, the broadcast fails the non-excludability requirement for a pure public good.
reference: 1.6 Classification of goods and services | 1.6.2 nature and definition of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Air outdoors may be a free good in one setting, while purified air in a sealed laboratory is supplied using scarce filters, electricity and labour. Which principle explains the different classifications?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether consumers have imperfect information.

options.label: B
options.text: Whether the government sets the price.

options.label: C
options.text: Whether provision involves an opportunity cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether society regards clean air as morally desirable, irrespective of the resources required to supply it in each location.

explanation: The laboratory's filters, electricity and labour have alternative uses. This opportunity cost distinguishes supplied purified air from naturally abundant outdoor air.
